issues.legal_issue: A stipulated period for completing a contract to sell immovable property does not, by itself, make time essential to the contract.
material_facts: The agreement concerned the sale of immovable property and required the purchaser to complete registration within a stated period, failing which the earnest money would be forfeited.
The agreement also provided that the purchaser could compel the sellers to execute the sale deed if they evaded doing so.
The agreement did not state unmistakably that time was essential, and the court found no sufficiently strong circumstances displacing the normal presumption.
issues.conclusion: Time was not of the essence of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: For a contract concerning the sale of immovable property, time is normally presumed not to be of the essence. Fixing a period for performance does not displace that presumption; sufficiently strong circumstances may do so. The Court applied Gomathinarayana Pillai & Ors. v. Palaniswami Nadar, [1967] 1 SCR 227, 233. No statutory provision is cited for this principle.

rule.if: sale_of_immovable_property_contract and fixed_performance_period and not unmistakable_time_essential_language and not strong_circumstances_showing_time_essential

predicates.sale_of_immovable_property_contract: The parties made a contract for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.fixed_performance_period: The contract set a period within which performance was to be completed.
predicates.unmistakable_time_essential_language: The contract stated unmistakably that time was essential to performance.
predicates.strong_circumstances_showing_time_essent: The circumstances were sufficiently strong to show that the parties intended time to be essential.

issues.definition: When a sale contract for immovable property sets a performance period but neither unmistakable language nor strong circumstances shows that time is essential, the rule treats time as not essential.

issues.legal_issue: Whether time is of the essence of a contract cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal when it was not specifically pleaded or made an issue at trial.
material_facts: The sellers did not plead at trial that time was of the essence of the contract.
No trial issue was framed on whether time was of the essence.
The appellate court nevertheless considered and decided that question.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was in error in allowing the sellers to raise the time-essentiality question in the absence of specific pleadings or a trial issue.
issues.legal_principle: A party may not raise in an appeal the question whether time was of the essence when that question was not specifically pleaded or made an issue before the trial court. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural principle.

predicates.appeal_from_trial_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court decree.
predicates.time_essentiality_not_specifically_plead: The party did not specifically plead at trial that time was essential to the contract.
predicates.no_trial_issue_on_time_essentiality: The trial court did not frame an issue on whether time was essential to the contract.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a trial decree, a time-essentiality argument is not considered when it was neither specifically pleaded nor made a trial issue.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who remains ready and willing to perform, takes steps to complete a sale, and is prevented from completing it by the sellers’ evasion is entitled to specific performance.
material_facts: The purchaser was a long-standing tenant of the property and paid earnest money under the agreement to buy it.
Before the completion period expired, the purchaser sent letters and notices seeking execution of the sale deed, offered to pay the balance and outstanding rent, and attended the registrar’s office.
The evidence accepted by the Court showed that the purchaser had sufficient funds to complete the transaction.
The Court found that the sellers evaded their responsibility to execute the sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was always ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, the sellers evaded their responsibility, and the decree for specific performance was restored.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the correspondence, the purchaser’s efforts to complete the transaction, and the evidence of available funds, and concluded that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform while the sellers evaded performance. It restored the trial court’s decree for specific performance. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this determination.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and purchaser_remained_ready_and_willing and purchaser_took_steps_to_complete and purchaser_had_sufficient_funds and sellers_evaded_execution

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.purchaser_remained_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations under the contract.
predicates.purchaser_took_steps_to_complete: The purchaser took steps to complete the transaction, such as requesting execution or attending to registration.
predicates.purchaser_had_sufficient_funds: The purchaser had sufficient funds to perform the purchaser’s payment obligations.
predicates.sellers_evaded_execution: The sellers evaded their responsibility to execute the sale documents.

issues.definition: In a suit for specific performance, where the purchaser remained ready and willing, took steps to complete the transaction, had sufficient funds, and the sellers evaded execution, the rule grants specific performance.
